Two defects the run exposed, both fixed the same day: `gate_command` written as a STRING dies with FileNotFoundError in the middle of the first task and gets reported as a task crash (now named by load_config and by doctor, before the run); and the spend label «дорогие роли (ревью+план)» became a lie the moment the executor's price entered the sum — a label that depends on config is not a label, so it is now just «дорогие роли». Third, unmeasured and written down as such: writer and judge are now one family, which removes the independence §3.2 leant on; the loop warns when the two models coincide, E13 must measure the size of the effect.

FIRST E13 MEASUREMENT — both arms run the SAME DAY on the same frozen set (BENCH-1, six greenfield tasks, E8's surviving stand reset to its red-state commit eed16f7), configs byte-identical except two lines. Arm A: kimi / kimi-code/k3-256k. Arm B: claude / claude-sonnet-5. Reviewer held CONSTANT (sonnet, effort medium, no pool — a lottery would have been a second factor), confirmations=1, memory off. RESULT: the two arms are indistinguishable on outcome — 6/6 closed, every task on the first iteration, zero scope violations, zero red gates, and ZERO findings from the reviewer on either arm. Implementation wall-clock 148 s (A) vs 142 s (B) on first attempts — inside noise. Review of the resulting diffs: $0.535 (A) vs $0.591 (B), i.e. claude's diffs cost 10 % MORE to review, the same author-moves-the-reviewer's-bill effect E8 saw in the other direction (K2.7 diffs +29 % over K3). Executor price: $0.676 for arm B, UNKNOWN for arm A — not zero, unmeasurable, paid in quota. THEREFORE total cost is NOT comparable on this bench, and the honest conclusion is the one ADR-002 predicted three weeks ago: trivial greenfield tasks cannot discriminate executors, because both converge in one round and the reviewer finds nothing to say. E13 needs a brownfield set before it can decide anything. What it DID settle: the engine switch is operationally neutral — same outcomes, same speed, no new failure mode attributable to the engine.

THE BENCH FOUND A BIGGER LEVER THAN THE ONE IT WAS MEASURING. Across both arms 5 of 17 reviewer calls (29 %) failed to produce a valid verdict, burning $0.67 — 37 % of ALL review spend on this bench, and more than the entire difference between the two engines. Two distinct modes, both on claude-sonnet-5 at effort medium. (1) PLACEHOLDER APPROVE, 2 cases: the model returned a schema-shaped verdict reading literally {"analysis": "Test", "verdict": "approve", "summary": "Test", "findings": []}. This is the first live catch by the substance guard (MIN_ANALYSIS=40 / MIN_SUMMARY=20 in verdicts.validate_verdict): without it a fake approve would have waved code through with a clean journal. (2) STRUCTURED-OUTPUT RETRY EXHAUSTED, 3 cases: the model packed the ENTIRE verdict into the `analysis` string as pseudo-XML (`…</analysis>\n<verdict>approve</verdict>\n<summary>…`), the CLI rejected it, the model retried by rewriting prose (`width<1` -> `width<1` -> `width меньше 1`) instead of fixing the SHAPE, and the CLI's own retry cap ran out. The reviewer prompt contains no XML tags — the shape is invented by the model. Loop behaviour was correct throughout: one silent retry rescued 4 of 5, and the fifth (b4wr on arm B, two dead calls in a row) was blocked with an inbox question instead of being guessed at. NOT deterministic: the same reviewer on the same diff produced a valid approve on the third call after `swarm retry`. Live consequence to weigh: the pilot's confirming rounds draw from a pool that includes exactly this model and effort. Candidate fix, NOT applied (it would change the loop mid-experiment): salvage — when structured_output is absent but the last StructuredOutput call carries a parseable verdict blob, recover it, the same principle that made parsing.report_in tolerate the executor's preamble.

AN ARM THAT IS NOT PINNED IS NOT AN ARM. Setting up E13 exposed that the swarm passes `-m` to kimi ONLY when `executor_model` is configured — and the pilot stand never configured it. So for the whole of PILOT-1 the executor model was whatever ~/.kimi-code/config.toml called default_model, a machine-level setting outside the experiment, outside git and outside every journal line. That default has since moved from `k3` (1M) to `k3-256k` (owner's change, same direction as ADR-010's quota work), which means E8's arm A (K3 1M) and any fresh unpinned run are different models with identical-looking records. Both E13 arms therefore pin the model explicitly, and the k3-256k choice rests on ADR-010's parity claim within 256k — this bench's context is under 25k, far below either window. Nothing was measured wrong on purpose; the point is that nothing in the loop's own records could have told us.

E13 ROUND 1 CLOSED with both arms complete. b4wr, the one task the reviewer defect had blocked on arm B, was requeued (`swarm retry`) and closed on its first iteration, so both arms now stand at 6/6 and BOTH STANDS PASS THEIR FULL SUITE independently of the loop (47 tests, zero skips — every contract filled). Final accounting separates executor work from the overhead of someone else's defect, because a round replayed after a block is not a fix round: rounds are keyed by (task, iter), and two rows sharing an iter mean one round played twice. EFFECTIVE EXECUTOR WORK: A 148 s / price unknowable; B 146 s / $0.686. REVIEW THAT PRODUCED A VERDICT: A $0.535, B $0.591. OVERHEAD OF THE REVIEWER DEFECT: A $0.359 (two dead calls, both rescued by the silent retry), B $0.414 ($0.313 dead calls + 21 s / $0.102 of executor work replayed after the block). FULL STAND SPEND: A $0.894, B $1.691. Findings: zero on both arms, all six tasks, both stands — the bench discriminates nothing about quality, exactly as ADR-002 predicted for greenfield micro-tasks. The engines differ in one measurable way only: on arm B every dollar is visible, on arm A the executor's price does not exist as a number.

A QUESTION THAT CAN NEVER BE ANSWERED. When a task is blocked with an inbox question and then returned to the queue by `swarm retry` instead of by an answer, the question survives its own task: `swarm answer q001 …` refuses with «вопрос принадлежит завершённой задаче: ответ не возвращает её в очередь» and records NOTHING, while `swarm status` keeps printing «вас ждут 1 вопрос(ов) — очередь не пойдёт дальше без решения» over a queue that is finished, 6/6. The refusal is half right — answering must not silently reopen a closed task — but dropping the answer is not the other half. The question is a RECORD of what happened; the diagnosis of the reviewer defect had nowhere to go except this findings file. Proposed fix (not applied, it changes the inbox contract and deserves its own decision): record the answer against the closed task and close the question, printing that the task was not reopened; and let `status` distinguish «questions blocking the queue» from «questions left over from tasks that closed by another route».

REVIEWER CONTRACT FAILURE FIXED, and the fix is measured against the real failures rather than against fixtures alone. Three changes, each answering one observed mode. (1) SALVAGE: when the envelope carries no structured_output, the last StructuredOutput tool call is pulled out of the stream, its fields unpacked if the model crammed them into `analysis` as pseudo-XML, and the result run through the SAME validate_verdict as any other verdict — no leniency: a findings list that does not parse is NOT an empty list (substituting [] would turn request_changes into approve), and a verdict outside the closed enum is refused. Journalled as `verdict_salvaged` with a `salvaged` flag in metrics, because a verdict obtained around the normal channel must stay distinguishable from one that arrived through it. (2) INFORMED RETRY: the second attempt now carries the reason the first was refused. validate_verdict was reduced to `verdict_problem(v) is None` so the check and its explanation cannot drift apart — otherwise the retry would be told a reason nobody rejected it for. The note goes in the very TAIL of the prompt, behind the diff: in the stable prefix it would void the task's whole prompt cache (§8), and the first call stays byte-identical (pinned by test). (3) EVIDENCE: a task requeued by `swarm retry` restarts round numbering and reused the same log filename — on E13 the replay erased the stream of the very failure that needed reading. The envelope keeps its name (the board and `swarm why` read it); the stream moves to a free name beside it. MEASURED ON THE REAL STREAMS: repair returns 2 of the 4 surviving failures ($0.24 directly) and removes the one task block, which had cost a further $0.175 of replayed work plus the wait for a human. The two placeholder cases are NOT rescued and must not be — there is nothing there to rescue. Bench frozen at experiments/goldset/verdicts/ (8 cases, 4 real + 4 synthetic negatives, in the gate); the bench is two-sided on purpose, since a one-sided one would push the code toward inventing verdicts. Gate 1094 tests.

THE PLACEHOLDER APPROVE IS ROUTINE, NOT A FLUKE — third occurrence in ~20 calls. The live smoke that validated the fix (one task, claude executor, sonnet/medium reviewer, 2026-08-22 evening) reproduced it unprompted: review attempt 1 returned {"analysis": "test", "verdict": "approve", "summary": "test", "findings": []} with terminal_reason `completed` — a well-formed, schema-valid, entirely empty approval of code it had not discussed. MIN_ANALYSIS=40 caught it, the informed retry named the reason, and attempt 2 came back with a real approve for $0.079 instead of $0.240. That is the whole argument for the substance guard in one run: the schema would have passed this, the journal would have shown a clean approve, and the orchestrator would have committed on the strength of the word «test». Worth stating plainly because the guard is cheap and its absence is invisible — nothing in a green run tells you it is missing.

A QUESTION THAT COULD NOT BE ANSWERED, FIXED. Found while closing E13: when a blocked task is returned to the queue by `swarm retry` rather than by an answer, its inbox question outlives it. `swarm answer` refused — and discarded the answer with the refusal, so the diagnosis of what had happened had nowhere to go — while `swarm status` kept printing «очередь не пойдёт дальше без решения» over a queue that was 6/6 done. The guarded invariant was right and is kept: an answer must not resurrect a closed task, because an unconditional return to pending sends finished work back to be redone. What was wrong was the price. Now: the answer is RECORDED (journal row carries `reopened: false`, the decision accumulates in the task's human_decisions so a later retry — and E9's memory — still see it), the task's status is untouched, and the CLI says plainly that only `swarm retry` reopens. Classification is mechanical: `questions(blocking=True)` returns only open questions whose task is not done, and that is what «queue won't move» now counts; stale ones get their own list in status and a mark in inbox. Deliberately NOT treated as stale: a question whose task vanished from tasks.json entirely — a lost or plan-replaced queue would then hide every live question, and that failure is worse than the defect. Also hardened while there: the closed-task scan reads the queue as DATA (a hand-edited row that is a string, not an object, used to crash `status`). Gate 1106 tests.

NEGATIVE, MEASURED, AND REVERTED: symbol-level evidence exists for the boundary linter's last unreachable dispute and still cannot be used. The gap: q016 wants zeus-import-qet/src/convert.rs for task s2ky, and the two files share no path substring at all — the linter never saw it (rank 24 of 25). Hypothesis: a name DEFINED inside the boundary and used outside is a code dependency, not a word coincidence. It is real — convert.rs references `CURRENT_FORMAT_VERSION` and `Component`, both defined in zeus-model (inside the boundary) and both rare by the linter's own rarity filter. Implemented as a fourth signal (`producer`), matched CASE-SENSITIVELY so `Component` the type is not confused with `component` the word, and the tree walk was split into two reads (own files first, for their declarations) at no extra I/O. Then the frozen bench priced it, weight by weight: OFF 4/7@6 with q016 at 24; weight 0-2 → 4/7@6, q016 at 21 (evidence added, score unchanged); weight 4 → 3/7@6 (q017 6→8, q020 8→14); weight 6 → 3/7@6 (q005 2→6, q017 6→17, q020 8→19). The curve says one thing plainly: about twenty other files carry an equally rare symbol link to any given task, so the signal cannot discriminate, and buying q016 costs two disputes that were already caught. This is the SAME shape as the 2026-08-20 class-weight negative — raising a class raises its competitors too — reached this time from a genuinely new kind of evidence. Reverted: a signal that moves a rank from 24 to 21 and nothing else does not earn its complexity (§1.4: the losing variant is deleted). CORRECTION to the record: earlier docs named q005/q016 as the unreachable pair; the bench says q005 sits at rank 2 and the actual pair is q014 and q016. Both classes ARE reachable in other instances (q005 at 2, q017 at 6) — it is these two cases that are unreachable, not the classes. Probe kept for reuse: the sweep must override the module instance load_planner() builds inside measure(), or every weight silently measures the same run.

E13 ROUND 2 ON BROWNFIELD — the set ADR-002 demanded. BENCH-2 (six tasks that edit existing code with regression risk, full suite as the gate) replayed from its own red-state commit, both arms the same day, configs byte-identical except two lines, reviewer held constant at sonnet/medium. Result: arms again indistinguishable — 6/6 closed on both, every task on the first iteration, zero scope violations, ZERO findings on either arm. Executor work 305 s (kimi) vs 224 s (claude); review of the resulting diffs $0.734 vs $0.692; executor price $0.841 on B and unmeasurable on A. But the interesting number is the comparison with the SAME task set run 2026-08-07: that run produced 10 findings and needed second and third iterations (implement rows by iter: 11/4/1). Same tasks, same red state — and today's reviewer sends nothing back. So brownfield did not fail to discriminate; the JUDGE did. The bench's discriminating power is bounded by the reviewer arm, not by the task set, and that hypothesis was testable without re-running a single executor: the diffs were already committed.

THE PAIRED RE-JUDGE ANSWERS E13, AND THE ANSWER IS A TIE. New instrument `experiments/bench/e13-rejudge.py`: re-review already-committed diffs with a different reviewer arm, building the prompt with the loop's OWN promptbuilder.review_prompt (a home-made prompt would measure the harness, not the reviewer) and reading the envelope through the same parser, salvage included. No executor is re-run, so the design is paired — one diff, two hands — and cheap. Ran opus/xhigh over all twelve brownfield diffs. ARM A (kimi/k3-256k): 6 findings, all minor, 6/6 approve, $2.466. ARM B (claude/sonnet): 6 findings, all minor, 6/6 approve, $2.470. Six and six, minor and minor, within $0.004 of each other. Stronger still: on r1cf BOTH arms drew the same finding (the docstring's Turkish-I claim is wrong — casefold is locale-independent) and on r5rp both drew the same one (the docstring promises "" for empty text while width<1 raises). Two different engines, same spec, same residual defect: what is left over belongs to the TASK, not to the executor. CONCLUSION for E13: on small, well-specified tasks — greenfield and brownfield alike, 12 tasks total — the executor engine does not change the outcome, the rounds, or the quality the reviewer can see. What it changes is measurability (arm B's price exists as a number) and dependence (arm A's price is paid in a quota that ran out). The reviewer arm dominates the executor arm by a wide margin: 0 findings for $0.73 versus 6 findings for $2.47 on the SAME diffs, i.e. 3.4x the cost buys the only findings anyone gets.

THE VERDICT-CONTRACT FAILURE IS A PROPERTY OF THE ARM, NOT OF THE PROMPT. Round 2 measured the same rate as round 1 with the fix live: 2 of 8 reviewer calls invalid on each arm (25 %), $0.34 and $0.345 burned. The fix did what it promised and no more — on arm B the salvage engaged once and correctly REFUSED what it recovered (a placeholder), and no task was blocked this time — but the waste is unchanged, because the model still answers wrongly a quarter of the time. The comparison that names the cause: in the paired re-judge, opus/xhigh returned 12 valid verdicts out of 12 on the same kind of diffs and the same prompt builder. Same contract, same schema, same task class — zero failures. So the 25-29 % is sonnet-at-medium-effort, not the reviewer prompt, and the cheapest remaining fix is not more code: it is the arm. Worth weighing against the pilot's confirming pool, which draws from {opus, sonnet}/medium — a quarter of those confirming calls are expected to cost money for no verdict.

MUTATION AUDIT OF EVERYTHING SHIPPED 2026-08-22/23, and it found two holes. Sixteen mutations, one invariant broken at a time, each expected to turn the gate red: executor engine (unknown name silently defaulting, prefix losing to key, git deny list emptied, kimi argv order drifting, an absent price substituted by 0.0), verdict salvage (an unparseable findings list becoming [], the substance threshold removed, the retry losing its reason, the failed stream being overwritten again, salvage disappearing from the journal), the inbox (an answer resurrecting a closed task, a stale question blocking the queue again, an answer to a closed task being discarded), and the run preflight. Fourteen were caught on the first pass. TWO WERE NOT, and both mattered: (1) `valid = salvaged or validate_verdict(...)` — the entire safety of salvage rests on the recovered verdict getting NO leniency, and nothing pinned it; the gold-set bench tested repair and validation separately but never the wiring between them. (2) removing the engine preflight from `swarm go` — the preflight had tests, but only through `run`, and `go` is the entry that spends money on planning BEFORE the first task. Both closed with tests the same hour; the audit now catches 16 of 16. The script is kept as a living instrument (`tools/swarm/mutate.py`, in the lint scope, named in CLAUDE.md): a new subsystem appends its mutations, and a mutation that stops being caught must be either fixed or deleted together with the defence it names. Note for whoever runs it: it edits sources in place and restores them, so the tree must be clean — and pytest must run with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, or a cached bytecode of the unmutated file reports a false 'not caught' (the same trap check.sh already documents).

E11 STARTED WITH ITS METER, NOT ITS FEATURE. The experiment's decision criterion is mutation survival of arm-A tests vs arm-B tests, and that number did not exist for either arm — so the instrument came first (same order E12 imposed on itself). `experiments/bench/mutation-survival.py` mutates a stand's sources one AST node at a time (comparison flips, arithmetic swaps, boolean swaps, dropped `raise`, bumped integer and boolean constants), runs the stand's own suite, and counts what the suite noticed. Two design choices are load-bearing. It deep-copies the tree per mutant, because mutating in place would fuse mutations into one. And it PRINTS EVERY SURVIVOR with file, line and substitution instead of a bare rate: some survivors are equivalent mutants that no test could kill, and only a human tells them apart — «survival 13 %» without the list is a number nobody can act on. Distinct from tools/swarm/mutate.py, which holds hand-written anchors to the loop's own invariants; for someone else's code you cannot author anchors.

ARM A MEASURED ON WORK ALREADY PAID FOR, and it has a hole. BENCH-3 (stand-b3) is the corpus where the executor wrote its own tests — four feature-tests tasks. Whole stand: 113 mutants, 98 killed, 15 survived (13 %). But the number that matters is the split by AUTHORSHIP. Modules whose tests were written beforehand as fixtures (BENCH-1/2: roman, ngrams, csvline, distance, wrap, tokens, report): 97 mutants, 11 survived, 11 %. Modules where the executor wrote BOTH the code and its tests from scratch (cli.py from s4cli, normalize.py from s3nm): 16 mutants, 4 survived, 25 %. Every one of the four survivors is in cli.py and every one is a REAL hole, not an equivalent mutant: the default `top = 10` can become 11, the default `width = 72` can become 73, and the boundary `if width < 1` can become `<= 1` or `< 2` — all four pass the suite untouched. So the executor's own tests exercise the paths it wrote and skip the defaults it chose and the boundary it guarded. That is precisely the failure E11 predicts, and it now has a number instead of four anecdotes. CAVEATS, stated because the sample is small: 16 mutants is a thin base; normalize.py contributes only 2 of them; rank.py and stats.py are excluded from the clean split because they carry BOTH pre-authored and executor-authored tests, which is a confound, not a result. Arm B has to beat 25 % on the same modules to mean anything.

THE FIRST ARM-A NUMBER WAS MEASURED AT THE WRONG COMMIT, and fixing it made arm A look WORSE while revealing a better example of the effect. The 25 % figure came from stand-b3 at its final state — but by then two LATER tasks had touched the same modules (s7nc unified error messages across normalize/tokens/cli, s9te added test_errors.py as regression tests for those messages). Arm B will only ever reach the state right after s4cli, so the paired baseline must be read there too. Re-measured at 22b88d9 (immediately after s4cli): 16 mutants, 11 killed, **5 survived — 31 %**. The extra survivor is the interesting one: in normalize.py the explicit `raise TypeError` can be deleted and the executor's own test_normalize.py does not notice, because the test asserts only that SOME TypeError appears — and with the guard gone `unicodedata.normalize` raises TypeError by itself. So the type contract survives while the promised message ('normalize_text: ожидается str, получено …') silently disappears. CLASSIFICATION, because the rate alone would mislead: 4 of the 5 survivors are unambiguous holes (two chosen defaults and the width boundary in cli.py, none exercised by any test); the fifth is only WEAKLY a hole — the observable type is preserved and only the diagnostic degrades. Honest reading: 31 % raw survival, 25 % unambiguous. And the fifth was eventually caught — not by its own author, but by a separate later task written for a different purpose, which is itself the E11 argument in miniature. Arm B must be measured at the same commit depth to compare at all.

THE TESTER'S PROMPT CONTAINS A FALSE PREMISE, AND THE RUN EXPOSED IT ON TASK ONE. I told the tester «tests must fail today (nothing is implemented) and pass once the spec is implemented». Checked mechanically by replaying its six tests for s1ch against the code as it stood BEFORE the executor: FIVE PASSED, one failed. That is not hollow testing — it is the task. s1ch adds CACHING to an existing `word_freq`, so every correctness property (same results on repeat, no shared mutable dict handed out, cache key must respect `fold`) is a property that must be PRESERVED, and it already holds before the change. Only the speed assertion could be red. So for any task whose subject is a non-functional change — caching, performance, refactoring — «your tests must be red» is false, and a tester obeying it literally would have to invent artificial failures. This one did the right thing and ignored the instruction where it did not apply, which is luck, not design. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE ROLE, not for this run: the prompt must distinguish tasks that ADD behaviour (tests start red) from tasks that PRESERVE behaviour while changing how it is achieved (tests start green and are regression guards). Deliberately NOT fixed mid-experiment: changing the prompt between arms would make the measurement meaningless (one factor per run). Noted as the first change for E11's round 2. Side observation on the same evidence: the tester's cases list names an aliasing bug — handing the caller the cached dict itself — which is a real defect class an implementation-first author rarely tests for.

E11 ROUND 1 MEASURED: the independent tester wins on mutation survival and loses on price. Same four feature-tests tasks (s1ch, s2tn, s3nm, s4cli), same starting commit, same four modules, arm A replayed at the commit arm B reaches so no later task's tests count for A. ARM A (executor writes its own tests): 37 mutants, 11 survived — 30 %. ARM B (independent tester writes them first, never seeing an implementation): 27 mutants, 6 survived — 22 %. Per module A->B: stats 25->13 %, rank 40->25 %, normalize 50->0 %, cli 29->43 %. Volume does not explain it — 28 tests in arm A against 32 in arm B. Mutant COUNTS differ (37 vs 27) because the implementations differ, so only rates are comparable; the tool says so on every run. PRICE: arm B cost $4.48 on this run — tester $2.34, executor $1.01, review $0.72, plus $0.42 burned on reviewer contract failures. The tester alone is more than twice the executor. Arm A's own run (2026-08-07, different loop version) shows $2.79 of review with the executor's price unmeasurable on kimi, so the two totals are not directly comparable — what is comparable is that arm B ADDS a whole role's cost, and here that role cost more than the work it guarded.

THE METRIC IS WRONG UNLESS IT IS SCORED AGAINST THE SPEC, and arm B proved it by predicting its own survivors. Arm B's cli.py looks WORSE than arm A's by mutation survival (43 % vs 29 %), which is the opposite of the experiment's hypothesis on the very module where arm A had four real holes. Reading the survivors settles it: two of arm B's three are `return 2` -> `return 3` — the process exit code on bad arguments. The task spec says only «некорректные аргументы обрабатываются без трейсбека» and «ненулевой код»; it never fixes WHICH non-zero code. And the tester SAID SO IN ADVANCE, in the `unclear` field of its report: «точное числовое значение кода ошибки … спецификация фиксирует только код выхода и без трейсбека, поэтому тесты проверяют только code != 0». The mutation survived exactly where the tester had declared the spec silent. Arm A pins `2` — not because it tested better, but because the same author chose 2 and then asserted its own arbitrary choice. By the contract, arm A is OVER-FITTED and arm B is correct; by the raw metric, arm A wins. CONSEQUENCE: a mutant that changes only UNSPECIFIED behaviour is an equivalent mutant with respect to the contract, and the score must exclude it. The `unclear` field turns out to be the mechanism for doing that mechanically — the tester hands you the list of positions where a surviving mutant is expected. That was not why the field was added; it was added so an ambiguous spec would be a finding instead of a guess.

E6 WAS ABOUT TO BE DECIDED IN FAVOUR OF EMBEDDINGS BY A COMPARISON THAT NEVER HAPPENED. Replaying the pilot's real retrievals showed FTS returning EXACTLY ZERO rows on every single query while the vector supplied 100 % of the hits — which reads as a clean win for embeddings until you ask why. Cause: `websearch_to_tsquery` joins terms with AND, and the loop passed it the whole task spec. The condition became «one lesson contains ALL of these dozens of words», which is never true against an 8-row corpus. Proof it is the query shape and not the corpus: `корпус` alone returns 2, `эталон` 1, `решения владельца` 5 — but `корпус ERC-03` returns 0, because ERC-03 appears in no lesson and one absent term zeroes the whole conjunction. FIX: build the query from salient words joined by websearch's own `or` (data still travels as a parameter, no SQL splicing), lower-cased, deduped, words under 4 letters dropped, capped at 12. SAME queries after the fix: 3-5 hits each instead of 0. Now measured properly on the pilot's 16 executor retrievals: FTS supplies 65 of 80 hits, the vector adds 15 on top — i.e. the design's «FTS first, vector as a coverage net» is finally TRUE, having been «vector only» in production since the feature shipped. Two consequences beyond E6. The embedder was called on every single retrieval, because `len(hits) < k` held trivially at 0; now it is called only when FTS underfills. And any earlier reading of `queries.jsonl` that concluded «the vector is what works» was measuring a defect.

E9's PREMISE HOLDS: memory retrieves the right lesson for every task that has one. Before paying for two live arms (off vs executor), the cheap question is whether memory even surfaces the relevant lesson — if it cannot, rounds-to-convergence is not worth measuring. Dry replay over the pilot's 16 closed tasks, building the exact block `inject_block("executor", …)` would hand the executor, with no model call: a non-empty block for 16 of 16 tasks (1290-1831 chars, inside the 2000-char budget), and for all FIVE tasks that own an anchored lesson, THAT lesson is in the block — 5/5, including k3ad, the task where the loop three times repeated work the owner rejected. HONESTY ABOUT THE DETECTOR: the first version of this replay reported 0 of 16 because it read anchors as `{"value": …}` when the real shape is `[{"kind": "task", "ref": "m6pe"}]` — it silently returned an empty task id and measured itself. The block visibly contained the lesson id all along. Rule taken from it: a detector that reports ZERO must be run against a known positive before its zero is believed. Live arms are now worth running — but only after the FTS fix above, since the arms would otherwise have measured a vector-only retriever.

TWO STANDS CANNOT HOLD INDEPENDENT COPIES OF THE SAME LESSONS, and the A/B protocol demands exactly that. The protocol says «restore the memory snapshot before each arm», which implies two stands carrying the same corpus. In PG they cannot: the lesson id is a CONTENT fingerprint and the table's primary key, so copying the pilot's lessons into a second stand and running `memory reindex` inserts nothing — every row conflicts on id and the upsert merely updates the existing one. Observed exactly: reindex reported «8 rows for stand X» while `SELECT count(*)` stayed at 8 and every row still carried the FIRST stand's name. Consequence for anyone reusing lessons across stands: the second stand retrieves NOTHING from PG (its repo filter matches no rows) and silently degrades to the local file scan — a different retriever than production, which is the one thing an A/B must not vary by accident. Worse, in the SHARED database the collision does not merely lose rows: it touches the pilot's corpus. The fix used here is a separate database per experiment (`memory_db`), with the memory-free arm additionally set to `memory_index = "manual"` — index upkeep is not the measured factor and an off arm has no business writing at all. Design note for later: making the key `(id, stand)` instead of `id` would let stands share content without sharing rows; the counter «confidence from repetition» would then need to be per-stand or aggregated deliberately, which is a decision, not an oversight.

E9 EXECUTOR ARM, ONE TASK, AND THE SIGNAL IS IN THE KIND OF FINDING, NOT THE COUNT. Task v9lb («выводами УГО владеет библиотека») run twice from an identical starting commit, isolated clones, memory the only varied factor, reviewer held at the pilot's own opus/xhigh. ARM A (memory=off): 8 findings — correctness 4, ARCHITECTURE 3, style 1; 2 major. The three architecture findings are design questions («не сказано, может ли один и тот же вывод каталога быть размещён на нескольких УГО одного компонента»), the loop classified them as intent and escalated to the human: task ends `ask_user`, the queue stops, $4.20 spent. ARM B (memory=executor, 2 lessons injected per call, 1597 and 1681 chars, ids in the journal): 7 findings — correctness 5, style 2, **ARCHITECTURE ZERO**; the loop kept working, the executor fixed them and went to round 2, $5.93. The design ambiguities that stopped arm A did not arise when the executor had the owner's 2026-08-16 decisions in front of it. That is precisely the hypothesis: memory stops the loop re-litigating what the owner already decided. HONEST WRINKLE, because it cuts the other way: arm B had MORE majors (4 vs 2). Memory did not make the work better overall — it changed WHAT the reviewer had left to say, from «what should this even do» to «this is wrong here». UNMEASURED: rounds to convergence. Arm B's round-2 review died as a process before returning a verdict (`review_failed`), which is infrastructure, not memory — arm B was still progressing when it stopped. n=1 task; the other two idea-tasks were never reached because a single open question halts the queue.

THE E6 FIX IS WHAT MADE THIS MEASUREMENT POSSIBLE, and it was made hours earlier for unrelated reasons. During arm B the embedder was unreachable — DNS failure, `socket.gaierror: nodename nor servname provided`, logged as «эмбеддер не ответил» and swallowed fail-open exactly as designed. So retrieval had no vector at all and ran on full-text search alone. Before this morning's fix FTS returned ZERO rows on every real query (websearch_to_tsquery ANDs the terms, and the loop passed it a whole task spec), which means arm B would have injected NOTHING and the experiment would have compared memory-off against memory-off — silently, with the journal still printing `memory_injected` counts of zero that nobody would have questioned. Instead the journal shows 2 lessons and 1597/1681 chars injected per call. Two lessons worth keeping: a fail-open dependency going dark is exactly when the fallback path gets exercised for real, so the fallback has to be the one you actually tested; and a defect fixed for one experiment (E6) silently decided whether another (E9) could be measured at all.

MEMORY CARRIED THE FILE NAMES AND NEVER SHOWED THEM. Looking for a task on which E9's executor arm could actually be measured turned up a natural experiment: `zeus/crates/zeus-erc/tests/corpus_erc.rs` tripped the scope guard THREE times across TWO tasks — k3ad twice, then s2ky. And the timeline is decisive: k3ad's lesson, which carries that exact file in its anchors, was written 2026-08-18 18:42; s2ky ran afterwards and tripped on the same file. The knowledge existed. Injection was off, so nobody read it. Setting the replay up exposed why it would not have helped even with injection ON. The block handed to the executor renders the lesson's PROSE only. Anchors — the grounding data, the part that says WHICH FILES the decision touched — were never rendered, and worse, `search_fts`/`search_vec` did not even SELECT the `anchors` column, so nothing was there to render. A lesson reading «boundaries extended to convert.rs, components.rs and the zeus-erc engine» reached the executor without a single file name: the operative half of the decision was dropped. Fixed on both levels — the projection now fetches anchors, and the block prints a «файлы урока» line. Verified end to end: the same query now shows `tests/corpus_erc.rs` in the block for task s2ky, which is precisely the file it tripped on. A CONFESSION ABOUT THE CAP: my first path cap was 4, and corpus_erc.rs is the FIFTH anchor — the cap hid exactly the file the experiment exists to test. Raising it «because mine did not fit» would be the same tuning-to-the-answer already rejected by measurement in the boundary linter, so the new cap of 6 is justified from the corpus instead: lessons that carry paths carry 5, 5 and 4 of them, so six shows a file list whole and still truncates a pathological one.

THE PAIRED s2ky REPLAY PRODUCED NO SIGNAL ABOUT MEMORY, and the reason is instructive. Two arms, same task, same commit (ee53c217), same three pre-s2ky lessons, differing only in experiments.memory (off vs executor). Arm A: 3 rounds, $6.80. Arm B: 2 rounds, $6.18. That looks like a win for memory and is not one. The task was CHOSEN because the original s2ky run tripped the scope guard on zeus/crates/zeus-erc/tests/corpus_erc.rs, and the injected lesson names that exact file among its anchors — a mechanical, non-judgemental signal. NEITHER ARM TRIPPED SCOPE. The hypothesis had nothing to fire on. Arm A's extra round came from `cargo fmt` plus a missing rustdoc line on ZEUS_KEY_NAMESPACE that clippy -D warnings rejected; its own round-3 report says the implementation 'was already in place and correct'. Lint hygiene is exactly the class of variance a single-task A/B cannot separate from the factor under test, and the injected lesson (do not change UUIDs/designators/traversal order) has no bearing on it. Calling the one-round difference a memory effect would be a false causal story bought for $12.98. The design error is mine and is nameable: I picked the task by looking for a mechanical signal in a PAST run, and did not ask whether that signal reproduces under a DIFFERENT executor engine. The original trip was kimi's; both arms here ran claude/sonnet. A replay that changes the engine is not a replay of the condition that produced the signal.

BOTH ARMS LOST THEIR FIRST ROUND TO THE $3 PER-CALL CEILING AND THE LOOP CALLED IT A CRASH. The envelope is unambiguous — is_error:true, terminal_reason:'budget_exhausted', subtype:'error_max_budget_usd', total_cost_usd:3.01, errors:['Reached maximum budget ($3)'] — but the CLI also exits non-zero, the driver names the round 'crash' from the return code, and executor.claude_outcome only re-read terminal_reason when the reason was already 'done'. So the one path that can actually occur never reached the mapping. Cost of the wrong word is not the metric but the DIAGNOSIS: 'crash' sends the operator to look for a dead process; the truth is 'raise executor_budget_usd or split the task'. Worse, the futile-round feedback then told the executor its answer 'contained no valid JSON report — repeat, respecting the contract', which is false and expensive: the edits were on disk and the advice sent it to redo paid work. Rule extracted: THE ENVELOPE'S OWN ACCOUNT OF WHY IT STOPPED OUTRANKS THE EXIT CODE, because a real crash leaves no envelope at all — that absence is the whole difference. Fixed in engines.budget_truncated (reads terminal_reason AND subtype; planner.py already knew both spellings, the executor path knew one) with the retry note split by cause. Three tests, two of which fail on the pre-fix code. Note the second-order cost: nearly half the experiment's $12.98 went to two rounds that produced nothing and were then misnamed in the journal.

E9's executor arm now has two measured tasks and no answer. v9lb (2026-08-23): architecture/intent findings fell 3 to 0 with memory while majors rose 2 to 4, and rounds-to-convergence was unmeasurable because review died as a process. s2ky (today): rounds differed by one, attributable to lint hygiene, and the mechanical signal the task was chosen for never fired in either arm. Two tasks, two different reasons for inconclusiveness. The honest reading is that a per-task paired A/B on this loop cannot resolve an effect of this size: the round count is dominated by whether the executor happened to run cargo fmt. Either the metric has to move to something memory can plausibly shift (disputes per task, repeat dead ends across a QUEUE rather than a task), or the arm needs a queue long enough that hygiene noise averages out — and at ~$6.50 per task per arm, a 10-task paired queue is ~$130. That is a budget decision, not a technical one, and it belongs to the owner.

SCORING AGAINST THE SPEC DOUBLES THE INDEPENDENT TESTER'S MARGIN. Raw round-1 numbers were arm A 11/37 survivors (30%) vs arm B 6/27 (22%) — a 27% relative reduction in holes. Every survivor, and every mutant caught in the same positions, was then classified against the spec TEXT into real_gap / equivalent / spec_silent, and the last two classes removed from BOTH denominators together with their catches (dropping only survivors would gift a point to whichever arm has more such positions). Result: A 5/28 (18%) vs B 2/23 (9%) — a 50% relative reduction. Both rates fall but not equally — A by 40% (30->18), B by more than half (22->9) — and that asymmetry is the second result: raw mutation survival was measuring the spec's silence and the generator's generosity as much as it measured tests. All FOUR of arm B's dropped mutants were survivors in positions the tester had itself declared in `unclear` — arm B had zero unexplained survivors. Arm A dropped 9 (2 equivalent, 7 spec_silent), of which 3 were CATCHES: it pinned `return 2` three times, a value the spec never fixes, by reading its own implementation. Classification lives as data with a reason per row (experiments/goldset/e11/classification.jsonl) because it is judgement and must stay arguable. Correction made the same hour: the first draft of this row said 'both more than halve'. The gate test froze the actual ratios and refused it — the claim had been written before it was computed.

THE 'SHARED BLIND SPOT' WAS NOT A BLIND SPOT. The one mutant surviving in both arms (rank.py:18, `n <= 0` -> `n < 0`) was reported as a common weakness that authorship could not explain. It is unkillable: at n == 0 both implementations return [] down either path — arm A through `n >= len(freq)`/sorted-of-empty, arm B through heapq.nsmallest(0, ...). Verified by enumeration: 9031 input pairs per arm, zero differences. Same for arm A's rank.py:21 (`n >= len(freq)` -> `>`): equivalent on 11730 pairs. A third claim fell with them — the 2026-08-23 note calling all four of arm A's cli.py survivors 'real holes, not equivalent mutants' was wrong about `if width < 1`, a boundary the spec never states. RULE: an equivalence claim must be ENUMERATED, not argued, and a survivor list nobody has justified against the spec text is a list of suspects, not of holes. The wrong claim stood for a day because nothing forced each survivor to be defended.

THE IMPLEMENTER'S TESTS MISSED THE SPECIFIED THING AND CAUGHT THE UNSPECIFIED ONE. The s4cli spec states exactly two constants outright: `--top N (default 10)` and `--width W (default 72)`. Those are precisely the two mutants that survived arm A (10->11, 72->73) and precisely the two that arm B killed. Conversely the exit code `2`, which the spec never names, is what arm A pinned (3 catches) and arm B deliberately did not. The hollow-test failure mode in one line: tests written by the author of the code assert what the code happens to do and skip what the specification asked for. Four anecdotes across the program argued this; it is now a number on a paired corpus.

THE MOST EXPENSIVE ROLE IN THE LOOP CARRIED A $1 CAP NOBODY ASKED FOR, AND 1155 GATE TESTS NEVER NOTICED. reviewer.py passed `--max-budget-usd str(config.get('review_budget_usd', 1.0))` unconditionally — so a stand with no money settings at all still ran its reviewer under a one-dollar ceiling. It fired in practice: 'ревьюер обрублен по бюджету' is a named diagnosis in the loop's own list. Proof the hole was in the TESTS and not just the code: when the flag was removed, the full gate stayed green — nothing asserted its presence. Owner's decision the same day made spending='money_bin' the default (no implicit per-call cap anywhere), with the invariant that an EXPLICIT cap outranks the mode in both directions — a setting that silently stops applying is the failure class the whole closed key list exists to prevent. Explicit 0 reads as 'remove the cap', not 'truncate immediately', or zero would be a trap. The run budget stays never-implicit: what a goal is worth is the owner's call. 16 tests + 4 mutations added.

MEASUREMENT MOVES FROM PAIRED STANDS INTO ORDINARY WORK, and the reason is two failures of the old method rather than a preference. The paired stand answered E9's planner arm and E13's engines; it failed TWICE on E9's executor arm, both times about method: on one task the round counter is dominated by whether the executor happened to run `cargo fmt`, and an honest paired 10-task queue costs ~$130 for a single question. Worse than the price: the task is chosen by a human under an expected signal — s2ky was picked for a scope trip that then did not occur. Ambient mode draws the factor per task on real work that would have been paid for anyway. Honest downside, stated in the tool itself: the sample is UNPAIRED — different tasks per arm, between-task variance is not subtracted, so it is weaker than a stand at small n and wins only on count. Hence three guards: the analyser REFUSES to name a winner below 8 tasks in the smaller arm; it recomputes each draw from (seed, factor, task_id) and DISCARDS observations that do not recompute (warning-then-counting them anyway would contradict itself in adjacent lines — caught in my own first draft); it prints spread, not just means. Draw is deterministic per task so a replay lands in the same arm; one factor only (two random factors give inseparable effects — arithmetic, not caution); a factor also pinned by an explicit flag is a startup REFUSAL, since the journal would otherwise record a draw that never happened and it would surface only weeks later as numbers that do not add up.

THE OWNER SAW 'STRICT RULES VS CREATIVITY' RUNNING THROUGH THE EXPERIMENTS. The axis is real but sits elsewhere: it is not two temperaments to split across agents, it is ONE agent that finds an ambiguity and then silently closes it, so the finding never reaches the human. Four independent pieces of evidence already collected: the s3nm trap asked this in so many words ('will the executor set the boundaries itself and document them, or silently pick an arbitrary reading'); E11 measured it (arm A pinned its own invented exit code and missed the two constants the spec states outright, arm B did the reverse and declared the gap in `unclear`); E9's executor arm showed memory supplying answers and intent findings falling 3 to 0 — the questions stopped being asked; the boundary linter found 3 of 7 real disputes have no textual trace at all, so no rule can predict them. Both poles ALREADY exist in the loop but as side-jobs of roles with other work (strict: `unclear`, scope guard, gate, verdict schema; creative: dispute, plan-diff, ask_user). So E14 asks whether splitting them into roles beats the current fusion — and registers the CHEAPER counter-hypothesis first: promote `unclear` out of the tester into a standalone cheap pre-pass, since today the list only appears when a tester runs and the tester cost $2.34 on the E11 round, more than two executors. Not implemented on purpose: the programme's own rule is a dual variant and a decision criterion BEFORE building, and the loop already has four expensive roles. It is the first experiment measurable ambiently, needing no paired stand at all.

OWNER CORRECTED MY READING: 'inject the experiment into regular work' meant TWO EXECUTORS IN PARALLEL on the same task, and explicitly not to save money. That is a better design than the ambient draw I built, and it fixes the exact weakness I had documented: the ambient sample is unpaired, so between-task variance is not subtracted. A duel gives a PAIRED observation on ordinary work — one task, one commit, one spec, both arms at once — and wall-clock is the slower arm rather than the sum, while nobody chose the task. It removes the stand's weakness (human picks the task under an expected signal) and the ambient draw's weakness (unpaired) simultaneously. THE HONESTY RULE IS THE WHOLE DESIGN: the live arm is drawn in advance and never re-picked by outcome. Keeping whichever arm passed the gate would measure max(A,B) — the 'arm B rate' would stop being a property of B and become a property of selection; better code, worthless data. So the live arm runs in the normal tree exactly as today (nothing after implement() knows a duel happened, and with the flag off behaviour is byte-identical), while the shadow arm runs in a git worktree purely to be measured and its work is NEVER adopted. Both arms get gated — 'did this arm's work pass' is the metric. Rescue-the-live-arm-with-the-shadow is named in the doc and deliberately NOT built: it is the same selection, and it would need an explicit exclusion rule.

THE MUTATION AUDIT CAUGHT THE ONE INVARIANT THAT MATTERS MOST, IN MY OWN NEW TESTS. The mutation 'the live arm is always on instead of drawn by lot' SURVIVED — that is precisely the honesty property the whole duel design rests on. Cause: my test asserted the draw over four hand-picked task ids (d1, zz, s2ky, q017) and all four happened to draw 'on', so the assertion was vacuous. Fixed by enumerating 60 ids and separately asserting that BOTH arms occur as live. This is the same rule already recorded on 2026-08-23 for the E9 replay detector — a detector that has not seen both outcomes is measuring itself — and I re-learned it 24 hours later in a different subsystem. Worth noting the audit is what found it: 27 of 28 caught, and the one that escaped was the important one. A test suite that is green tells you nothing about which invariants it defends.

E14's CHEAP COUNTER-HYPOTHESIS IS BUILT (unclear.py, flag [experiments] unclear). One short call per task before any work, returning only the LIST of decisions the spec does not make, which then rides into the executor prompt with one requirement: if you must choose, NAME the choice in `deviations`. The mechanism converts a SILENT invention into a DECLARED one, which is exactly the difference E14 sets out to measure. Three prompt decisions all aimed at false positives: an empty list is declared a success in so many words (specs are often complete, and an invented fork is worse than none — it costs the executor attention and looks like work in the measurement); answering its own questions is forbidden (whoever finds the gap must not be able to close it); a gap noticeable only by READING THE CODE is declared a false positive, because that is an implementation's choice rather than the spec's silence — the same discipline as E11's tester. The list does NOT go to the inbox: a question to the human on every task would stop the queue, and the measurement needs work to continue; the executor's `dispute` channel already exists for a fork that genuinely blocks. An empty list produces no prompt block at all, since 'no gaps' costs tokens every round and says nothing. With the flag off the executor prompt is byte-identical — pinned by test.

THE FIRST REAL RUN OF DUEL+PURIST FOUND FOUR DEFECTS THAT 1206 GREEN TESTS DID NOT. Cost of finding them: $0.96 and about twenty minutes on a scratch Python stand. (1) `engines.report_from_envelope` hard-required a `status` field — the EXECUTOR's contract — so the purist's valid schema-checked answer was discarded. The purist found exactly the fork planted in the spec, the loop paid for it, threw it away, and told the human 'the spec left no forks'. Saying 'no gaps' when you mean 'no answer' is the worst possible failure: it sounds like knowledge. Fixed by making the identifying field a parameter. (2) The shadow arm's exception was swallowed whole — no reason, no traceback, nothing in the journal — despite my own docstring in the same function promising 'its failure must leave a trace'. The diagnosis had to be assembled from which files were ABSENT. Fixed with a required error hook. (3) Both arms wrote their raw stream to the same path `{task}-i{n}-executor.jsonl` from two threads; the shadow clobbered the live one. Same class as the two reviewer verdicts that once overwrote each other. Fixed with a per-arm log tag. (4) below.

THE HAND-ROLLED MODULE LOADER WAS A LATENT RACE, AND CONCURRENCY MADE IT REAL IMMEDIATELY. The loop's seven flat loaders all publish a module into sys.modules BEFORE executing it — the standard recipe, required for the circular agents<->loop import. Single-threaded that costs nothing. The duel runs two arms in threads, and the first clean run died with `module 'obs' has no attribute 'get_logger'` — not a typo and not a missing function, but a second thread seeing a half-executed `obs` in sys.modules and taking it for finished. THE FIX HAD TO BE ONE LOCK, NOT SEVEN: the modules are shared, so thread A loading `obs` via agents._load and thread B loading it via codemap._load never touch the same per-module lock. New dependency-free `modlock.py` holds a single RLock plus a `ready()` that checks spec._initializing — presence in sys.modules is NOT proof the code ran. Reentrant because loading is nested: executing obs.py can itself hit another _load. Worth noting the general shape: adding concurrency does not create these bugs, it collects the ones already there, and they surface as nonsense errors far from their cause.

DUEL AND PURIST PROVEN END-TO-END ON REAL WORK, $0.96. One task on a Python stand with a deliberately open spec ('teach wrap_text to handle a word longer than width' — never saying whether to split, overflow, or hyphenate). The purist found 3 forks, naming the planted one first: what should the result LOOK like, split or whole, with or without a hyphen. The duel ran both arms in parallel in separate git worktrees: live arm (memory off) committed 49 lines, shadow arm (memory executor) wrote 57 lines in 1 file and PASSED ITS OWN GATE, and the two raw streams landed in separate files. That is a genuine paired observation on ordinary work — the thing two paid stands failed to produce for E9's executor arm. Note what the duel does NOT do here: the shadow's 57 lines are discarded, on purpose, because the live arm was drawn in advance. Keeping the better-looking arm would measure selection instead of the factor.

THE E14 MECHANISM FIRED FOR THE FIRST TIME ON REAL WORK, AND IT IS VISIBLE IN THE EXECUTOR'S OWN WORDS. On v9lb the purist ($0.47) found 3 forks in a spec whose own text says the task 'awaits format design'. The executor then declared, in `deviations`: «Спецификация явно оставляла три развилки нерешёнными (см. 'What the spec does NOT decide') — сделал и задокументировал выбор по каждой в §7а». It named the prompt block by its heading, chose on each fork, and wrote the choices into the document as a numbered section. That is a silent invention converted into a declared one — the exact mechanism E14 exists to test, working end to end. NEGATIVE HALF, equally important: it did NOT prevent escalation. The task still ended `ask_user` with 4 intent findings, and the architecture-finding count did not drop versus the 2026-08-23 arm-A run of the same task (3 then, 3 now). n=1.

THE PURIST AND THE REVIEWER FIND DIFFERENT THINGS, AND THE SPLIT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN ACCIDENTAL. Of the reviewer's 3 architecture findings on v9lb, exactly ONE is downstream of a fork the purist had named: the purist asked whether an unbound component blocks release, the executor decided YES, and the reviewer objected that tier 3 then 'describes no way out of that state'. The other two could NOT have come from the purist by construction — «§9 still titled 'v1.5 framework' though §7а made library_cache.toml normative now» and «the flat Device record loses LIB-1's device→variant level» are both contradictions against the REST OF THE REPOSITORY (docs/01, LIB-1/LIB-3, section headings), and the purist is explicitly forbidden from reading anything but the spec. So the two roles are not substitutes and the cheap one cannot absorb the expensive one: the purist finds forks INSIDE the spec text, the reviewer finds collisions BETWEEN the change and everything else. Note the shape of the surviving overlap too — the reviewer's objection is now an argument about a DECLARED decision rather than about an unexplained one. Whether that is worth $0.47 a task needs more than one pair.

FIRST PAIRED OBSERVATION FROM A DUEL ON REAL WORK: v9lb, $7.30 total. Both arms produced a report and BOTH PASSED THEIR OWN GATE; the shadow arm (memory=executor) wrote 2 files, +235/-8, in its own worktree, and its work was discarded as designed. Cost split: purist $0.47, live executor $2.34, shadow executor $2.76, review $1.73 — so the duel cost about 1.7x a plain run, not 2x, because the purist is cheap and the single review is shared. THE ACCOUNTING DEFECT THIS EXPOSED: both executor calls wrote identical `phase=implement` metric rows, so $2.76 of MEASUREMENT was indistinguishable from work in `total_spend()`. The sum was not wrong — that money is real and must count — but the meaning was: a budget where the instrument looks like a second worker tells the operator nothing about what they bought. Fixed by tagging the shadow row with `arm="shadow"`. Also confirmed: the live arm reproduced the 2026-08-23 arm-A behaviour on the same task (intent findings, ask_user), which is a small piece of evidence that the loop is reproducible across a month and a config rewrite.
